🚀 APOLO 404 | Innovación sin límites

Somos un equipo apasionado por la ciencia, la tecnología y la exploración espacial. Participamos en NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 con el propósito de desarrollar una solución innovadora para monitorear la salud de los astronautas.

Nos enfocamos en programación, inteligencia artificial, análisis de datos y diseño tecnológico. Valoramos la creatividad, el compromiso y el trabajo colaborativo.

APOLO 404: Beyond Earth, Beyond Limits.
summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web app that helps mission planners decide where and when to land near the lunar south pole. For 15 candidate sites, including the Artemis III regions and the IM-2 Athena landing site, it rebuilds the real horizon seen from the ground using NASA LOLA elevation data out to 200 km. It then traces the paths of the Sun and Earth every hour from November 2026 to December 2028 with NAIF SPICE (DE440) ephemerides. From this it computes the two things a lander needs to survive: power (how much sunlight reaches the site) and communications (when Earth is visible). Users can explore each site in a 360° panorama or a 3D view with real shadows, compare up to three sites, and use the "Mission delayed" mode to get the best alternative sites and dates in under a second. Our Sun and Earth positions match JPL Horizons to within 0.00003°. This matters because at the pole, a few hundred meters or a few days can decide whether a mission has light and contact with Earth.
details:
What it does

Lunar Landing Site Navigator shows what a lander would actually see at 15 candidate sites near the lunar south pole: the NASA Artemis III candidate regions, Shackleton's rim and Mons Mouton, where IM-2 Athena landed.

- Explore: a polar map of the sites. For each one, a 360° panorama shows the real terrain horizon with the Sun's path (gold) and Earth's path (blue, dashed), animated through time, plus eight metrics (sunlight %, longest day and night, Earth visibility %, hours to sunset and Earthset, next Earth window, Sun at landing) and a 30-day timeline of light and contact.

- Compare: up to three sites side by side on the same date.

- Mission delayed: enter the original landing date, the delay and a tolerance. The app scores every site and landing time (every 6 h) with adjustable weights and hard filters, and returns the 10 best options in under a second, each with its three main reasons.

- 3D and 360° views: the local terrain lit by the real Sun with shadows, and an immersive panorama from 2 m above the ground.

- Validation: every comparison and assumption is visible in the app.

- Available in English and Spanish.

How it works

1. Terrain: LOLA elevation models from NASA's PGDA at 5, 10, 20 and 240 m/px. We cast rays every 0.5° of azimuth with exact spherical geometry, out to 200 km, to build the real horizon at observer heights of 1, 2, 5 and 10 m.

2. Ephemerides: NAIF SPICE (DE440) gives the Sun and Earth positions every hour from November 2026 to December 2028, converted to local azimuth and elevation.

3. Metrics: each hour we compute what fraction of the solar disk is above the real horizon and whether the Earth is visible. The metrics run in the browser, so the ranking is instant; the same code exists in Python and a test checks that both agree.

4. Site points: published reference points often fall on steep slopes, so each site is moved to the best-lit point with slope of 8° or less within 1 km. The reference and the rule are shown in the app.

Validation

- Sun and Earth positions match JPL Horizons to within 0.00003°.

- The horizon algorithm matches analytic test cases within 0.02°.

- Illumination is compared with Mazarico et al. (2011), and the IM-2 Athena landing is reproduced: Sun 2.47° above a 0.83° horizon, consistent with the low-Sun conditions reported.

Benefits and expected impact

At the south pole the Sun never rises more than a few degrees, so a few hundred meters or a few days decide whether a mission has power and contact with Earth. The navigator turns raw NASA data into answers a planner can use right away, especially when a launch slips and the landing site or date must be re-chosen quickly.

Tools

Python (numpy, numba, pyproj, rasterio, spiceypy) for the data pipeline; TypeScript with React, Vite, D3 and three.js for the web app; deployed as a static site on Vercel. NASA data: LOLA DEMs (PGDA 78, 81, 90), NAIF SPICE kernels, JPL Horizons, Artemis III candidate regions and LROC.

Creativity and factors considered

Instead of a static illumination map, we show the horizon as an astronaut would see it, with the real paths of the Sun and Earth, and answer the practical question "what if we land later?". We prioritized scientific accuracy (no synthetic data, everything validated), transparency (assumptions are shown and editable), speed (everything runs in the browser) and accessibility (bilingual, works on mobile).

Limitations and next steps: horizons are precomputed, so arbitrary coordinates would need a backend; next we plan more sites, multi-year statistics, an exportable mission report and thermal risk layers.

https://apolo404-alunizaje.vercel.app/
